4. //! Kernel frame type.
5. //!
6. //! A [`KernelFrame`] represents a single page-sized physical frame allocated for kernel use.
7. //! It provides `Deref`/`DerefMut` for direct kernel access (identity-mapped) and frees the
8. //! underlying frame on drop via the global frame allocator.
9. 
10. //==================================================================================================
11. // Imports
12. //==================================================================================================
13. 
14. use vstd::prelude::*;
15. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
16. include!("kframe.spec.rs");
17. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
18. include!("kframe.proof.rs");
19. 
20. use crate::hal::mem::{
21.     Address,
22.     FrameAddress,
23.     PageAligned,
24.     PhysicalAddress,
25. };
26. use ::arch::mem;
27. use ::core::ops::{
28.     Deref,
29.     DerefMut,
30. };
31. use ::sys::error::Error;
32. 
33. //==================================================================================================
34. // Kernel Frame
35. //==================================================================================================
36. 
37. /// A type that represents a kernel frame.
38. #[derive(Debug)]
39. #[verus_verify(external_derive)]
40. pub struct KernelFrame {
41.     /// Frame address.
42.     base: FrameAddress,
43. }
44. 
45. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
46. verus! {
47. 
48. /// Abstract view of a kernel frame: the physical address of the owned frame.
49. impl View for KernelFrame {
50.     type V = int;
51. 
52.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int {
53.         self.base@
54.     }
55. }
56. 
57. } // verus!
58. 
59. // Dependency contract for the manager layer: wrapping a `FrameAddress` produces a handle whose
60. // abstract address is the same physical frame.
61. #[verus_verify]
62. impl KernelFrame {
63.     ///
64.     /// # Description
65.     ///
66.     /// Instantiates a kernel frame.
67.     ///
68.     /// # Parameters
69.     ///
70.     /// - `base`: Frame address.
71.     ///
72.     /// # Returns
73.     ///
74.     /// Upon success, a kernel frame is returned. Upon failure, an error is returned instead.
75.     ///
76.     // Dependency contract: wrapping a frame goes through `mm::virt::identity_map_page`, which
77.     // is outside the verification scope of `mm::phys`. On success the returned handle owns the
78.     // same physical frame that was passed in. `external_body` per `verus-ai-logs/tcb-allowed.md`:
79.     // the identity-mapping side effect lives in `mm::virt` and the body's `?`/log closures call
80.     // into that layer, so the wrap contract is trusted until `mm::virt` is verified.
81.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
82.     #[verus_spec(result =>
83.         requires
84.             base.inv(),
85.         ensures
86.             match result {
87.                 Ok(kf) => {
88.                     &&& kf@ == base@
89.                     &&& kf.inv()
90.                 },
91.                 Err(_) => true,
92.             },
93.     )]
94.     pub(super) fn new(base: FrameAddress) -> Result<Self, Error> {
95.         // Ensure the frame is identity-mapped in the kernel address space so that
96.         // Deref/DerefMut can safely access it. This lazily installs a page
97.         // table entry if needed (page tables come from a BSS pool, so no recursive frame
98.         // allocation occurs).
99.         let phys_addr: PageAligned<PhysicalAddress> =
100.             PageAligned::from_raw_value(base.into_raw_value()).map_err(|e| {
101.                 error!("frame base is not page-aligned: {e:?}");
102.                 e
103.             })?;
104.         crate::mm::virt::identity_map_page(phys_addr).map_err(|e| {
105.             error!("failed to identity-map frame: {:?}", e);
106.             e
107.         })?;
108. 
109.         Ok(Self { base })
110.     }
111. }
112. 
113. #[verus_verify]
114. impl KernelFrame {
115. 
116.     ///
117.     /// # Description
118.     ///
119.     /// Returns the base address of the target kernel frame.
120.     ///
121.     /// # Returns
122.     ///
123.     /// The base address of the target kernel frame.
124.     ///
125.     // Pure accessor: returns the owned frame's physical address unchanged. `result@ == self@`
126.     // gives `kpage` the exact address; `result.inv()` (page alignment carried from `self.inv()`)
127.     // lets `into_page_address` and the `KernelStack` arithmetic behind it proceed.
128.     #[verus_spec(result =>
129.         requires
130.             self.inv(),
131.         ensures
132.             result@ == self@,
133.             result.inv(),
134.     )]
135.     pub fn base(&self) -> FrameAddress {
136.         self.base
137.     }
138. }
139. 
140. impl KernelFrame {
141. 
142.     ///
143.     /// # Description
144.     ///
145.     /// Clears the target kernel frame.
146.     ///
147.     /// Uses the identity-map `memset` backend so that the write runs in the kernel address space.
148.     /// This avoids a page fault when the current CR3 points to a user page directory that lacks
149.     /// the PDE for this frame's physical address.
150.     ///
151.     pub fn clear(&mut self) -> Result<(), Error> {
152.         let base: *mut u8 = self.base.into_raw_value() as *mut u8;
153.         crate::mm::virt::memset(base, 0, mem::PAGE_SIZE).map_err(|e| {
154.             error!("memset failed: {:?}", e);
155.             e
156.         })
157.     }
158. }
159. 
160. /// # Safety
161. ///
162. /// `Deref` accesses the identity-mapped frame directly. The caller must ensure that the current
163. /// CR3 points to a page directory that has the relevant PDE for this frame's physical address
164. /// (i.e., the kernel page directory, or a user page directory into which the PDE has been
165. /// propagated via [`sync_kernel_pdes`](crate::mm::virt::sync_kernel_pdes)). For CR3-agnostic
166. /// writes, prefer [`KernelFrame::clear()`] which uses the identity-map `memset` backend.
167. impl Deref for KernelFrame {
168.     type Target = [u8];
169. 
170.     fn deref(&self) -> &Self::Target {
171.         let ptr: usize = self.base.into_raw_value();
172.         unsafe { core::slice::from_raw_parts(ptr as *const u8, mem::PAGE_SIZE) }
173.     }
174. }
175. 
176. /// # Safety
177. ///
178. /// See [`Deref`] impl — the same CR3 invariant applies.
179. impl DerefMut for KernelFrame {
180.     fn deref_mut(&mut self) -> &mut Self::Target {
181.         let ptr: usize = self.base.into_raw_value();
182.         unsafe { core::slice::from_raw_parts_mut(ptr as *mut u8, mem::PAGE_SIZE) }
183.     }
184. }
185. 
186. #[verus_verify]
187. impl Drop for KernelFrame {
188.     // Releasing the handle returns its physical frame to the global frame allocator via
189.     // `super::frame::free`, which is best-effort (`ensures true`) and `opens_invariants none`/
190.     // `no_unwind`, so `drop` makes no abstract postcondition. Callers (the manager error path,
191.     // `KernelStack::drop`) rely on this being the sole, complete deallocation step. Mirror of
192.     // `UserFrame::drop`.
193.     #[verus_spec(
194.         opens_invariants none
195.         no_unwind
196.     )]
197.     fn drop(&mut self) {
198.         if let Err(e) = super::frame::free(self.base) {
199.             #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
200.             error!("failed to free kernel frame: {:?}", e);
201.         }
202.     }
203. }
204.

3. impl KernelFrame {
4.     /// Well-formedness of a kernel-frame handle: its owned physical address is page aligned.
5.     ///
6.     /// Purely structural — it makes **no** ownership claim (it does not assert that the frame
7.     /// is allocated). Page alignment is the one caller-visible fact `base()`'s consumers rely on:
8.     /// `into_page_address` and the `KernelStack` index arithmetic behind it assume the returned
9.     /// `FrameAddress` is page aligned. Stated entirely on the abstract address `self@`, so it
10.     /// leaks no implementation detail. Mirror of `UserFrame::inv`.
11.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
12.         self@ % crate::hal::mem::spec_page_size() == 0
13.     }
14. }
15. 
16. } // verus!

1. # View Design: `mm::phys::kframe` (`KernelFrame`)
2. 
3. ## Abstract Resource
4. 
5. `KernelFrame` is an **owning handle to exactly one page-sized physical frame**.
6. To the outside world it is a single value: *which physical frame this handle
7. owns*. The only caller-observable abstract state is that frame's **physical
8. address**. Everything else — the identity-mapping side effect, how the address
9. is stored, the page-table mechanics, the byte contents reachable through
10. `Deref` — is internal or out of scope.
11. 
12. In-scope functions: `KernelFrame::new` (constructor), `KernelFrame::base`
13. (query), `KernelFrame::drop` (destructor).
14. 
15. ---
16. 
17. ## Inherited View (from upstream `mm::phys` manager verification)
18. 
19. ```rust
20. impl View for KernelFrame {
21.     type V = int;
22.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int { self.base@ }   // physical frame address
23. }
24. ```
25. 
26. This View was added when the manager layer (`alloc_kernel_frame`,
27. `alloc_many_kernel_frames`) was verified top-down. It is treated here as an
28. **input to evaluate**, not a finished design.
29. 
30. ### Evaluation against *all* callers
31. 
32. | Caller | Uses `self@` as… | Verdict |
33. |---|---|---|
34. | `manager::alloc_kernel_frame` | the allocated address: `kf@ == frame_addr@`, `lemma_kernel_alloc_one(..., result->Ok_0@)` | ✅ address |
35. | `manager::alloc_many_kernel_frames` | `kernel_frames_contiguous`, `kernel_addr_set(frames@)` — set/sequence of owned addresses | ✅ address |
36. | `virt::kpage::KernelPage::base` | `kframe.base().into_page_address().into_virtual_address()` — needs the address + page-alignment | ✅ address |
37. | `virt::kpage::KernelPage::frame_address` | returns `kframe.base()` verbatim | ✅ address |
38. | `Drop` sites (manager error path, `KernelStack::drop`) | identity of the frame being freed exactly once | ✅ address |
39. 
40. Every caller agrees: the abstract state is the **physical frame address**, an
41. `int`. No caller needs anything else.
42. 
43. **Decision: KEEP `type V = int` unchanged.** It already passes the
44. substitution test from every caller's perspective (see Rationale). Nothing is
45. renamed, added, or removed. The View definition is left exactly as inherited.
46. 
47. ---
48. 
49. ## View Struct
50. 
51. The View is a primitive, not a struct:
52. 
53. ```rust
54. impl View for KernelFrame {
55.     type V = int;                       // the physical address of the owned frame
56.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int { /* maps impl field -> address */ }
57. }
58. ```
59. 
60. - `view()` stays **`closed`**: public so callers write `kf@`, closed so the
61.   field-level mapping (currently `self.base@`) does not leak.
62. - The value space is `int` — the mathematical physical address. (Per the
63.   view-design exception, an address could keep `usize`; here the upstream View
64.   and the whole `FrameAddress`/`Inner` address algebra already work in `int`
65.   via `View::V = int`, so `int` is the consistent, cast-free choice.)
66. 
67. A wrapper struct (`KernelFrameView { addr: int }`) was considered and
68. **rejected** — see Rejected Alternatives.
69. 
70. ---
71. 
72. ## Well-formedness Invariant
73. 
74. `KernelFrame` currently has **no** `inv()`. Callers of `base()`
75. (`into_page_address`, and the page/stack address arithmetic behind it) rely on
76. the owned address being **page-aligned**. This is a caller-visible constraint
77. on the abstract state, so it belongs in `inv()`.
78. 
79. **Final decision (spec phase): single `inv()`, mirroring the verified sibling
80. `UserFrame::inv`.** The originally-sketched `internal_inv()` placeholder
81. (`pub closed spec fn internal_inv(&self) -> bool { true }`) was dropped: it would
82. be permanently `true` (the closed view `self@ == self.base@` already exposes the
83. alignment fact directly, so no implementation-consistency clause is needed), and
84. the `spec-design` skill discourages extra `pub spec fn`s on `impl MyType` beyond
85. `view`/`inv`. The result is identical in shape to `UserFrame`:
86. 
87. ```rust
88. impl KernelFrame {
89.     // Caller-visible well-formedness: the owned frame address is page-aligned.
90.     // Stated purely on the int view via the shared spec_page_size(); leaks no
91.     // implementation detail. Mirror of UserFrame::inv.
92.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
93.         self@ % spec_page_size() == 0
94.     }
95. }
96. ```
97. 
98. - `inv()` is **`pub open`** so callers can establish and consume it.
99. - `spec_page_size()` is the same `pub uninterp spec fn` already used by
100.   `FrameAddress::inv` (`self@ % spec_page_size() == 0`); reusing it keeps the
101.   alignment notion identical across the two types.
102. - No `internal_inv()` is defined; the alignment fact follows on the `new` /
103.   `base` paths directly from the required `base.inv()` / `self.inv()`.
104. 
105. No other `pub spec fn` is added to `impl KernelFrame` beyond `view` and `inv`.
106. 
107. ---
108. 
109. ## Spec Transition Functions
110. 
111. **There are none — and that is a deliberate, substitution-tested result.**
112. 
113. A `KernelFrame`'s abstract view is fixed at construction and **never changes**
114. for the lifetime of the handle. The in-scope API confirms this:
115. 
116. - `new(base)` is a **constructor**: it produces a fresh handle whose view *is*
117.   the input address. The contract is a constructor postcondition, not a
118.   transition on an existing view:
119. 
120.   ```rust
121.   // new (already external_body per tcb-allowed.md; keep its existing spec,
122.   // optionally surface the invariant it already guarantees):
123.   ensures match result {
124.       Ok(kf) => kf@ == base@ && kf.inv(),   // inv follows from required base.inv()
125.       Err(_) => true,                       // no ownership taken on failure
126.   }
127.   ```
128. 
129. - `base(&self)` is a **pure query** — no view change. Needed new spec:
130. 
131.   ```rust
132.   fn base(&self) -> (result: FrameAddress)
133.       requires self.inv(),
134.       ensures  result@ == self@ && result.inv();
135.   ```
136. 
137.   `result@ == self@` gives `kpage` the exact address; `result.inv()` (carried
138.   from `self.inv()`'s alignment clause) lets `into_page_address` and the stack
139.   arithmetic proceed.
140. 
141. - `drop(&mut self)` is a **destructor**. Its effect is *not* a transition on
142.   `KernelFrame`'s own view (the value is consumed). Dropping returns the frame
143.   `old(self)@` to the **global frame allocator**, so its postcondition is
144.   written against the allocator's View (`FrameAllocView` / `phys_view().frames`,
145.   the same View the manager already reasons over), e.g. "after drop,
146.   `old(self)@` is no longer allocated / is back in the free partition, and no
147.   other frame's status changes." Because that state lives in the allocator's
148.   abstraction, **no field is needed on `KernelFrameView` to express it**.
149.

151. view is immutable per handle, the only state change in the module
152. (allocation/free) is owned by the allocator's View.
153. 
154. ---
155.

this looks like it might be subsumed.
But
wait, I need to be careful about which inv() we're talking about. result
is a FrameAddress, so result.inv() is FrameAddress::inv, while self.inv() is KernelFrame::inv. If both
have the same definition (self@ % spec_page_size() == 0), and result@
== self@, then result.inv() is indeed derivable from the precondition and postcondition.
The question is whether this makes it truly redundant for the caller's purposes
, or if there's still value in stating it explicitly.
Actually
, I realize KernelFrame::view is marked closed, so the caller doesn't see the
mapping self@ == self.base@. But the caller does know result@ == self@ from the ensures clause, and they
know self.inv() == self@ % page == 0, so they can still derive result@ % page == 0 without needing to understand

the closed view. So result.inv() is subsumed.

I should verify the actual
FrameAddress::inv definition to confirm it matches before declaring this a strict reviewer catch.
Also, I'm noticing that error paths need meaningful ensures — returning true for Err(_) isn
't sufficient.
For
new specifically, it's an external_body function that doesn't actually touch the frame allocator at all, only
the page tables. So the frame is never consumed on either success or failure. The spec
